articles.title_zh: Faslane dry docks and research ship to be built in UK, says chancellor
articles.content_orig:
Orders for three floating dry docks, worth £6bn, to maintain the Royal Navy's nuclear-powered submarine fleet at Faslane will go to a UK-based shipbuilder, the chancellor has confirmed.
John Healey told the Labour conference the facilities were vital to national security and would support domestic shipbuilding as part of a "new age of industrialisation".
A UK-only bidding competition will decide who builds the floating docks but Navantia UK, which owns sites in Fife and Belfast, is seen as a frontrunner.
Healey has also pledged £115m for construction in the UK of a new marine research vessel to replace Cefas Endeavour, built by the Ferguson shipyard on the Clyde more than 20 years ago.
He told delegates in Liverpool: "I want to confirm today that we, this government will commit to £6bn of contracts for our British shipyards.
"They'll build the new docks for the submarines that will defend us all for decades to come, built in Britain by British workers because of the decisions of this Labour government."
The investment is part of a wider £15bn upgrade of the Faslane site, on the eastern side of Gare Loch, over the coming decade.
Scotland's first minister, John Swinney, who was visiting Montrose where two green energy projects are expected to create 160 jobs, said this was the kind of reindustrialisation he wanted, and he reiterated his opposition to nuclear weapons.
He said: "What I want to make sure is the chancellor takes an approach which is about investing in our economy, in our public services and in our infrastructure."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who was visiting Scotland, said he backed reindustrialisation but argued it could not happen until energy prices for industry came down.
"Today our industrial energy price is eight times that of America, twelve times that of China. With that handicap there is no chance of us reindustrialising," he said.
Floating dry docks are structures that can be submerged to allow a ship or submarine to enter. They are then raised and emptied of water, enabling inspections, maintenance and repair.
Unlike their land-based equivalents, their ability to float means they can be towed to different locations.
The last floating dry dock to be manufactured in the UK is believed to be Admiralty Dock 60, built in the 1960s and based at HMNB Clyde at Faslane until the late 1990s when it was sold for commercial use.
Currently the base has to rely on a single shiplift, an elevator-type device which hoists submarines out of the water inside a large maintenance building.
The Spanish state-owned shipbuilder Navantia has been lobbying hard to build the new floating docks for Faslane, through its UK division.
The company owns the Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast, along with fabrication sites at Arnish on the Isle of Lewis, Methil in Fife and Appledore in Devon.
Following Healey's speech, Navantia said it hoped to lead the project, using the Methil and Belfast facilities.
The GMB Scotland union has previously written to Healey asking for the work to be shared between the Methil site and Belfast.
Other possible contenders include the Cammell Laird shipyard in Merseyside, now owned by Balaena, and Babcock which has facilities at Rosyth.
Healey has also confirmed funding for a ship to replace Cefas Endeavour, the UK government's main fisheries and marine science research ship.
Operated by the Centre of Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas) the ship is based at Lowestoft in Suffolk.
Cefas Endeavour was launched in 2002 by the now nationalised Ferguson shipyard in Port Glasgow on the Clyde, and entered service the following year.
The firm could potentially bid to build the replacement as its size - expected to be up to 85m (279ft) - is well-suited to the yard's capabilities.
But Ferguson's is likely to face competition from other commercial yards such as Navantia and Cammell Laird.
Cefas Endeavour was a technically challenging ship, with exacting specifications for  noise and vibration so that it would not disturb fish during survey work.
Still in active service after 20 years, its replacement is expected to be delivered in the early 2030s.
Healey also used his speech to announce that Rolls-Royce will invest an extra £300m into its British factories in Derby, in Bristol, in Glasgow and in Rotherham.

articles.title_orig: Vikings send J.J. McCarthy to the Giants for a 2027 fifth-round pick
articles.title_zh: Vikings send J.J. McCarthy to the Giants for a 2027 fifth-round pick
articles.content_orig:
The Giants have added a new quarterback to the mix in the wake of Jaxson Dart’s season-ending injury .
Big Blue are acquiring J.J. McCarthy from the Vikings for a 2027 fifth-round pick, according to multiple reports.
McCarthy, 23, was the No. 10 overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, four picks after the Giants selected wide receiver Malik Nabers.
Get texts from Paul Schwartz with all the latest Giants news and insights, exclusive to Sports+ subscribers.
After leading Michigan to a national championship, McCarthy missed his entire rookie season due to a torn meniscus, struggled in 10 starts last year and lost the starting job to Kyler Murray this year.
He had been Minnesota’s third-string QB, with Carson Wentz starting in place of an injured Murray in Week 2.
McCarthy was coached at Michigan by Giants head coach John Harbaugh’s brother Jim, and the two spoke about the quarterback before the trade, according to Fox Sports’ Jay Glazer.
Jameis Winston started for Dart in the Giants’ rain-soaked Week 3 win over the Titans at MetLife Stadium and went 14-for-22 with 118 yards with zero touchdowns and zero turnovers. He was sacked three times.
The 32-year-old, who was the No. 1 overall pick by the Buccaneers in 2015, signed a two-year, $13 million contract extension before the season, a sign that the Giants had confidence in his ability to keep the ship steady if Dart were to get injured.
But his ugly effort in relief of Dart during a Week 2 loss to the Rams was cause for concern.
The only other quarterback on the Giants’ roster was Jake Haener, a 27-year-old 2023 fourth-round pick who had 39 career pass attempts, all in 2024 with the Saints. He was elevated from the practice squad for Sunday’s game.

articles.title_orig: Milania Giudice seen screaming at Teresa, called ‘danger to herself’ in police bodycam footage from airport clash
articles.title_zh: Milania Giudice seen screaming at Teresa, called ‘danger to herself’ in police bodycam footage from airport clash
articles.content_orig:
Teresa Giudice claimed that her daughter Milania Giudice had fentanyl in her system during the explosive airport clash, according to police bodycam footage obtained by Page Six.
The “Real Housewives of New Jersey” star told cops that Milania “had fentanyl in her system” while taking an elevator with Milania and her other daughter, Gia Giudice, during the Tampa International Airport incident last Wednesday.
“‘Cause I was laced, I go to college,” Milania, 20, fired back.
It is unclear if Teresa was saying that Milania had the drug in her system at that moment or at a previous time.
TMZ was the first to report the news.
Milania also told her parents that she posted the video of their explosive argument to her social media, prompting Teresa to tell her, “I don’t care anymore.”
“I want to save your life,” Teresa told Milania.
Start your day with Page Six Daily.
Elsewhere in the bodycam footage, Milania is captured raising her voice at Teresa and repeatedly yelling, “This is what we do now,” while her mom and older sister calmly try to reason with her to cooperate.
“Hurry up mom! Why don’t you run! “You wanted to cause a scene!” Milania shouts aggressively before yelling “Teresa Giudice” for others in the airport to hear.
Teresa replied gently to Milania, telling her that they were going to get on the plane together.
From there, the cops proceed to walk them to their gate.
In a private discussion between the police, one cop is heard confirming that Milania is “using repetitive language,” and another law enforcement official said she is a “danger to herself.”
“Yes, that’s why she got Baker Acted. They’re trying to get her back to a rehab facility,” another cop explains.
In another moment, Milania told Gia that she didn’t want the cops there anymore and asked them to “get away.” However, Gia tells Milania, “They are here to help.”
A different clip from the bodycam footage showed Milania eerily skipping away from cops as they followed her through the terminal.
Page Six has reached out to Milania’s rep for comment.
Last week, Milania posted and then deleted a video of her airport argument with Teresa and Gia.
“This is what we do now? This is what we do now?” Milania asked her family members, before Teresa replied, “I love you.”

United Kingdom police are releasing five terror suspects on bail Monday after they were arrested on suspicion of a terror plot targeting a U.S. air base in Britain this weekend.
Laurence ​Taylor, head of ​Counter Terrorism Policing, confirmed that investigations into the five men are ongoing, "including ⁠that this may be actively committed ​by proxies ​or ⁠individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on ⁠behalf ​of a ​foreign state." The Sunday night arrests came after a local resident and farmer in Gloucestershire told the BBC that she had called police late in the evening after coming across three white vans blocking a road near RAF Fairford air base. As she turned her car around, she told the BBC that her headlights illuminated a group of "hooded and masked men" who "panicked" upon being spotted and scrambled into a nearby woods.

articles.title_orig: Investigation of alleged gang-rape at Cornell University fraternity house reopened
articles.title_zh: Investigation of alleged gang-rape at Cornell University fraternity house reopened
articles.content_orig:
The investigation into an alleged rape at Cornell University in 2024 will be reopened, authorities said Monday.
The move comes after a lawsuit was filed earlier this month by a woman who claimed she was drugged and raped by multiple people at a fraternity house over the course of several hours.
"I have been asked by the community to revisit the decision whether to pursue criminal charges against the seven fraternity members. I have already begun that process, starting with our conversation with Jane Doe and her attorneys. Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means available – by testimony to the Tompkins County Grand Jury," Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said in a written statement.
"The Grand Jury will be able to consider the testimony of Jane Doe as well as any new evidence raised by the allegations of the civil complaint. Upon a vote by the Grand Jury to indict any or all of the individuals involved, this office will prosecute the charges zealously and to the fullest extent of the law," the statement continued.
According to the lawsuit, Doe was 20 years old in 2024 when she said she was drugged and raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house. Doe's attorney Thomas Giuffra claimed that following an investigation into the allegations, two of the accused were expelled, and there were no arrests.
Doe said she went to visit a friend at the frat house while she was intoxicated, and alleged she was pressured by two fraternity brothers into snorting what they said was ketamine.
A man then allegedly sent a message to the frat's Snapchat group chat suggesting a woman was available for sex. Doe says more men showed up after the message was out, and she was raped for hours.
Doe filed a report with the university's police department about three weeks later.
Van Houten however said that is not the version of events his office was told at the time.
"Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against  her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use  and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual," Van Houten said in a statement Monday. "My office obviously did not and could  not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be  filed until nearly two years later. Furthermore, I have never been contacted by Jane Doe's attorneys.  Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision.  Rather, I reached out to Jane Doe's attorneys after the lawsuit was filed to understand the  discrepancy between the original statement and the lawsuit's allegations and the proper path forward  in light of the lawsuit's allegations."
Van Houten said his office was contacted by police at Cornell University in November 2024 to review Doe's statement. He said his office was provided with a six-page document that was signed by Doe and that "the statement ... provides a different narrative and set of facts of the evens of October 19, 2024 than those alleged in the lawsuit."
Van Houten said it had nothing to do with whether or not the allegations would be difficult to prove.
"In this case, multiple prosecutors and criminal investigators reviewed Jane Doe's statement and  correctly determined the alleged facts as set forth in the statement do not constitute a crime. This decision  was not because the case would have been difficult to prove in court – it was because the facts as set forth in  the statement objectively prevent the filing of criminal charges. To be clear, the credibility of the woman,  who described the facts in excruciating detail, was never in question," Van Houten said.
Van Houten said he was not at present going to release the signed statement initially provided to his office. He provided a summary, however.
The Ithaca Police Department told CBS News New York the alleged incident was never reported to them, adding they are disturbed by the allegations.
Giuffra released a new statement after the DA's office said it would reopen the investigation.
"In the days following the assault, she was traumatized, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self preservation mode," Giuffra said.
Giuffra said she reported the incident to Cornell Police. Giuffra said Doe never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her initial complaint.
"It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted," he said. "I would have expected at the very least that she would have been interviewed several times and evidence collected by law enforcement and a case developed. This is the normal sequence for serious crime investigations."
"The defensive posture I have gleaned from the DA's statements leads me to believe that they recognize that there were failures and they are trying to excuse them. While I do not care for the attempt to blame Ms. Doe for these failures, we appreciate and support any efforts prosecute the parties responsible for the assaults and will fully cooperate with the District Attorney's Office to hold these men accountable," Giuffra added.
Cornell University released a statement about the reopening of the case.
"Cornell University supports the decision of the Tompkins County District Attorney (DA) to provide an opportunity for the victim's story in the 2024 Chi Phi fraternity sexual assault case to be heard by a criminal grand jury.
"Cornell also conducted a thorough Title IX investigation, which is separate from a criminal proceeding, over the course of several months. During that investigation, temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures were used. After investigation, and pursuant to federal law, the matter was sent to a hearing where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days. The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence. At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.
"In addition, the involved fraternity chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.
"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false. A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."
Cornell University previously said the school had launched a task force on sexual assaults, and set up a website where students can report bias, discrimination, harassment and sexual misconduct incidents.
The Chi Phi national headquarters sent CBS News New York the following statement following the initial lawsuit.
"The sexual assault allegations involving parties at Cornell University are deeply concerning. Anyone who reports sexual violence deserves to be heard and treated with compassion, dignity, and respect.
"Chi Phi unequivocally condemns sexual violence. Our founding principles of Truth, Honor, and Personal Integrity, and our mission of Building Better Men, call on every brother to demonstrate character through his actions and respect for the dignity and safety of others. Sexual violence is fundamentally incompatible with those expectations.
"We are aware of the lawsuit concerning an alleged incident in 2024. While we cannot discuss the specific allegations during pending litigation, we take this matter seriously. Our responsibility is to approach this with care for those affected and respect for a fair legal process."

articles.title_orig: Trump administration lowers fuel economy standards, critics say at a significant environmental cost
articles.title_zh: Trump administration lowers fuel economy standards, critics say at a significant environmental cost
articles.content_orig:
Traffic moves along the 405 Freeway on Feb. 13 in Los Angeles. Apu Gomes/Getty Images hide caption

The Trump administration announced Monday it's scaling back how fuel efficient American carmakers need to make their fleets.
The Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards set average fuel economy levels for carmakers. The revised rules, which were finalized Monday, will now require carmakers to make their new passenger car and truck fleets up to 1% more fuel efficient each year, aiming for an average of 34.9 miles to the gallon in model year 2031.
This is down from Biden-era rules, which required an annual 2% increase in fuel efficiency with a goal of most vehicles getting, on average, 50.4 miles to the gallon by 2031.
The rationale: affordability. Administration officials argue that fuel efficiency technology is expensive, and has helped to drive up the cost of vehicles. They estimate that scaling back the standards will shave about $1,300 off the sticker prices of new cars.
"This administration is delivering relief to families and reviving the beating heart of American manufacturing," said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in an online statement announcing the change.
President Trump weighed in over the weekend on Truth Social : "These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car."
Climate advocates and auto industry observers say the rules change is another step in the Trump administration's efforts to roll back Biden-era climate policies — including cutting the federal tax credit for electric vehicle buyers , delaying federal dollars for a nationwide EV charging program , and striking down federal waivers that let California set its own strict pollution regulations.
In a statement emailed to NPR, Dan Becker, director of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the Center for Biological Diversity, wrote that rolling back the standards would increase gasoline usage and pollution, "costing consumers at the pump and at the doctor's office."
"Trump is tanking sensible mileage standards at the worst possible time for consumers, who're getting hit with sky-high prices at the pump," he continued.
According to AAA , the national average price for gasoline today is close to $4.50 a gallon, and for diesel, a gallon is hovering close to $6.50, just short of last week's record high.
Easing CAFE standards will hinder the industry's realignment toward more fuel-efficient and electric vehicles, said economist Sue Helper, who studies the auto industry at Case Western Reserve University. "It's very bad in the long term, because it slows progress," she said. "Then we make our auto companies less competitive. We give them less practice in making the cars that both Americans will want in the future and that the rest of the world will want." After all, American carmakers hope to continue selling their cars in foreign markets that may have stricter emissions standards. And a future presidential administration could change the rules again.
CAFE standards have been part of the auto industry for decades. In 1975, during that decade's great oil supply shock, Congress enacted rules that encouraged carmakers to make their fleets more fuel efficient in an effort to reduce Americans' dependency on the Middle East for oil.
Since then, the national conversation about fuel efficiency has changed; the U.S. is now the world's largest oil producer, and many regulatory changes have instead been driven by concerns about climate change. Since the early 2010s, the fuel efficiency requirements for passenger cars and light trucks have consistently risen .
In practice, the Biden-era standards meant carmakers needed to make electric vehicles to balance out their gas guzzlers — otherwise they were subject to a fine.
But the Trump administration dropped that penalty last July as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, effectively defanging the Biden-era CAFE standards. In December, the White House proposed scaling them back altogether. Soon after, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened a period of public comment .
In its final rule announcing the change, NHTSA also said it's eliminating the ability of carmakers to trade credits amongst themselves for making electric vehicles — a part of the Biden-era CAFE Standards that Republicans often criticized. This rule allowed automakers to buy credits from EV manufacturers to offset making less fuel-efficient vehicles. This helped them meet their CAFE targets.
In announcing the new change, the administration said lowering the CAFE standards will make cars cheaper.
"Instead of allowing manufacturers to design and produce vehicles they believe their customers will want and need, while spreading real-world fuel economy improvements across their fleets, the system has increasingly led manufacturers to try to fit square vehicle pegs in round classification holes to force the adoption of technologies that do not meet the demands of American families," stated NHTSA in the final rule. "All of this adds inefficiency and cost — pushing even more consumers out of an already unaffordable new car market."
"It's true that the price of new cars has gone up quite a lot," says Helper at Case Western. But she contends that much of that is not because of fuel economy standards. Instead, she says, it's because vehicles have gotten larger, they've faced tariffs and supply chain issues in recent years, and they are often loaded with extras like infotainment systems.
A Consumer Reports analysis from 2023 found that between model years 2003 and 2021, vehicles got about 30% more fuel efficient, but attributed the rise in prices to an industrywide shift toward expensive SUVs, rather than from using more fuel-efficient technologies.
And when it comes to the monthly costs of a new car, there are external factors beyond a carmaker's control — like the cost of an auto loan , which is affected both by the Federal Reserve's benchmark lending rate and by an individual buyer's credit score.
"One of the cruxes of vehicle affordability right now is the average monthly payment getting jacked up, because interest rates are so high," says Ellen Hughes-Cromwick, who spent much of her career as Ford's chief global economist and now studies clean energy as a senior visiting fellow at the center-left Third Way think tank.
Plus, a cut in the sticker price might eventually be offset by spending on gas. If vehicles are less fuel efficient, that means drivers will need to fill up at the pump more often — which is especially salient in a year of high gas prices due to the war in Iran.
For now, American carmakers are stuck in a kind of jam.
On the one hand, Helper said, a rules change that makes it easier for them to sell trucks and SUVs is "good in the short-term, because they make a lot of profits making these giant vehicles," though they are not as popular outside of the U.S.
This new move "allows the U.S. more of a playground in this protected little Galapagos of an ecosystem where no one else is wanting to compete," Helper continued.
But the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a trade group representing car and light-truck manufacturers that sell vehicles to the U.S. and that includes automakers such as Ford, General Motors and Stellantis, praised the move. "We're still reviewing the final rule, but NHTSA made the right call to better align fuel economy standards with the law and current market conditions," said John Bozzella, president and CEO of the alliance, in an emailed statement to NPR.
"The standards finalized under the previous administration effectively required a switchover to electric vehicles that was out of step with market realities and customer demand. Today's final rule is an appropriate course correction," he continued.

articles.title_orig: Andrew Bailey, who joined FBI in unusual ‘co-deputy’ position, to leave bureau
articles.title_zh: Andrew Bailey, who joined FBI in unusual ‘co-deputy’ position, to leave bureau
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Another top FBI official is leaving the bureau after just a year on the job.
Andrew Bailey, who joined the FBI in the newly created position of “co-deputy director” in September 2025 to work alongside then-Deputy Director Dan Bongino, is stepping aside, two people familiar with the matter told NBC News. Bailey confirmed his move later Monday morning on social media.
An internal FBI email said Bailey was leaving for family reasons, the two people familiar with the matter said. Bailey had been the attorney general of Missouri before resigning his position to join the FBI last year. He had worked under FBI Director Kash Patel.
The FBI referred a request for comment to a post Bailey made on social media, stating that he wanted to thank President Donald Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel for the opportunity.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, we have delivered historic results in our mission to Make America Safe Again. With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri,” Bailey wrote . “I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence.”
Bongino, a conservative podcaster and former Secret Service member, subsequently left his job to return to podcasting after just under a year at the FBI. The nontraditional co-deputy structure, set up when Bongino was in the position, remained in place. Bongino was then replaced by Chris Raia, whose background as a career FBI special agent was more in line with the tradition of having the critical No. 2 position filled by someone with extensive knowledge of the bureau.
MS NOW first reported Bailey’s planned departure.
Patel, who is suing The Atlantic for $250 million over an article about his leadership at the bureau, has recently gotten into heated exchanges with Democratic members of Congress over his leadership at the FBI.
Ryan J. Reilly is a justice reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_zh: Dow drops more than 300 points, weighed down by rising oil prices and Treasury yields: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields edged higher on Monday as pressure on global government bonds resumed, amid higher oil prices and inflation fears.
The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield —the key benchmark for mortgage borrowing, auto loans and credit card debt — was up nearly 5 basis points at 5.23%.
The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, which is more sensitive to geopolitical risks, was roughly 4 basis points higher at 5.544%.
The 2-year Treasury note yield, which tends to react in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, moved up by more than 5 basis points to 4.918%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Bond yields elsewhere also moved higher as anxiety surrounding global government debt and sticky inflation continue to weigh on investors.
The yield on 10-year U.K. government bonds , known as Gilts, was 4 basis points higher, at 5.408%, while German 10-year Bund yields, considered a benchmark for eurozone debt, were last seen holding steady at 3.6277%.
Both French 10-year government debt and Japan's 10-year bond yield were more than 1 basis point higher early Monday.
The moves follow a volatile week for Treasurys. The benchmark 10-year note yield on Thursday reached its highest rate since June 2007 before easing, while the yield on the 30-year Treasury bond touched levels not seen since 2004.
As global oil prices moved higher on Monday — with West Texas Intermediate futures rising nearly 2% to $93.91 a barrel — investors are looking ahead to a flurry of fresh domestic economic data releases this week.
The latest monthly nonfarm payrolls data and unemployment rate are due out later in the week, following the core PCE index and latest quarterly GDP growth print. Before that, August's JOLTS report, expected Tuesday, is forecast to show job openings dipped slightly to 7.24 million month-over-month from 7.27 million in July.

articles.title_zh: SpaceX's Starship rocket orbiting Earth for first time after Texas lift-off - watch live
articles.content_orig:
The largest rocket developed by SpaceX has successfully reached orbit, marking an important milestone for the private aerospace company.
“Starship is orbital,” mission control announced to cheers on a livestream on Monday that showed the spacecraft’s launch from a base in Texas in the United States.
The uncrewed spacecraft almost didn’t achieve the long-desired goal after one of its engines shut down too soon. But with everything else working well and the bad engine no longer needed, flight controllers decided after several tense minutes to proceed as planned.
Founder Elon Musk’s showpiece rocket – the biggest and most powerful ever built – carried 26 of the latest and most advanced Starlink satellites to join the 11,000 older models already providing internet service. It was Starship’s 14th full-scale launch from Texas’s southern tip in three years. The earlier test flights ventured no farther than the Indian Ocean halfway around the world, often crashing in flames and briefly skimming space.
This time, SpaceX was intent on circling the globe from an altitude of 275km (170 miles) – not just once but six times over almost 10 hours, ending with a Pacific splashdown near Chile. The first-stage booster wasn’t meant to return to the Starbase launch site, either, instead dropping into the Gulf of Mexico within minutes of the morning liftoff.
SpaceX wants to ensure that everything works before flying Starship back to Starbase. If the spacecraft breaks apart over land and rains debris onto people, “our popularity would diminish very rapidly”, Musk said at a business summit earlier this month. “That’s why we’re being extremely cautious here.”
If all goes well with this orbital debut, the next Starship will return to the launch pad with giant mechanical arms grabbing the hovering spacecraft. If the catch works – Musk gives it even or slightly better odds – then SpaceX will re-fly the spacecraft by year’s end or early next.
The 124 metre (407-foot) rocket was designed from the start to be fully reusable – a key to lowering launch costs. SpaceX managed to salvage the last Starship from the Indian Ocean in July. Engineers modified the newly launched Starship’s heat shield based on hands-on inspections from the recovered spacecraft, which is being tugged back to Starbase.
SpaceX is pressing hard to certify Starship for orbital flight, a vital step towards moon and Mars travel.
NASA’s Artemis III mission is coming up as soon as next summer, and will feature a triple-launch docking exercise in orbit around Earth between an Orion capsule full of astronauts and competing lunar landers. Jeff Bezos’s Blue Moon will blast off first, then Orion – which will close in for a linkup – then Musk’s Starship for a docking with Orion once Blue Moon launches.
The next mission – Artemis IV, slated for no sooner than 2028 – would have astronauts landing on the moon in either Blue Moon or Starship, whichever is ready first. Subsequent moonshots will alternate between the two billionaires’ landers.
Musk originally developed Starship for Mars, intending to launch scores of them with the red planet’s first settlers. For now, he plans to focus on the moon and use Starship to haul satellites into orbit by the truckload, phasing out the company’s frailer Falcon 9 rocket within several years. A second Starship launch site is nearing completion at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center and a third is planned for the US state of Louisiana.

articles.content_orig:
• Liftoff successful: SpaceX’s Starship rocket, the most powerful rocket ever made, has launched from Starbase, Texas. The mission will seek to reach orbit for the first time during a 10-hour flight, deploying 26 operational Starlink satellites.
• What to expect: SpaceX will not attempt to land the Super Heavy rocket booster or return the upper Starship spacecraft to dry land. Both will aim for controlled splashdowns in the ocean.
• Coming up: SpaceX is facing intense pressure to get Starship ready for a crucial NASA test flight next year that could pave the way for the next moon landing.
You may have noticed that not all rocket-related headlines have been about the “ peaceful uses of outer space ” lately.
The United States recently revealed that it has deployed weapons into space for the first time, without saying what type of weapons or what they were intended to accomplish.
It’s only the latest in a long list of signs that space is rapidly becoming more militarized.
SpaceX has always played a massive role in supporting the United States’ strategic interests in orbit. The company famously once sued the US Air Force for the right to bid on rocket contracts ( and won ). The company now dominates the national security launch market.
And SpaceX’s space-based internet infrastructure has a national security bent of its own.
Starship’s task today was to deploy Starlink internet satellites that will help serve some of the company’s 12 million customers across 160 countries. But SpaceX is also using its space-based communications infrastructure to create a secure, military-grade network called Starshield for more than $6 billion.
Musk mentioned the secretive project during an August town hall, saying, “We can’t say too much about Starshield for obvious reasons — because it’s you know top secret and stuff — but the Starshield team has done amazing work, and it is now a vital part of America’s national security.”
The Department of War also recently announced it’s giving its workers access to Starshield AI’s Grok. (Grok, the AI model developed by xAI, is now part of SpaceX after a pre-IPO merger in February .)
Recent regulatory filings show that NASA administrator Jared Isaacman donated a whopping $3 million to President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. super Pac.
It’s a remarkably large donation and deeply unusual for a presidential appointee who is already confirmed to their post — espeicially a NASA appointee, as the space agency typically aims to position itself as apolitical.
NASA declined to comment on the donations, saying personal contributions fall outside the scope of the space agency’s communications duties. Isaacman told CNN that he has made “political and philanthropic donations” and declined to comment further on the matter.
Columbia law professor Richard Briffault, a campaign finance and government ethics expert, told CNN in an interview last week that there is nothing illegal about making such a donation — as unusual as it is. But it does raise ethics concerns, at least from an optics standpoint.
“It goes to the question of appearances: Is this an independent public servant serving the public interest, or is this somebody who is acting as a politician?” Briffault said.
This isn’t Isaacman’s first major donation to a Trump PAC. Last year, when Isaacman was attempting to get his nomination to lead NASA reinstated, he donated about $2 million to MAGA Inc. (Trump initially pulled the nomination, as CNN reported, because Isaacman had previously donated to Democrats. It was later reinstated, and Isaacman was confirmed in December.)
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has a preexisting relationship with Isaacman, as the Isaacman has paid SpaceX to fly him on two missions to orbit. Isaacman has repeatedly said he would not favor SpaceX in his official capacity.
Musk has also closely aligned himself with Trump and donated millions to MAGA Inc. But recently, Musk also expressed some regret about taking such a substantial role in campaigns.
“I got too involved in politics,” he told The Economist during a recent interview.
SpaceX will not allow Starship to stay in orbit for 10 hours, as the company had originally planned.
Mission controllers, during a recent “checkpoint” analysis, decided to end the mission a bit early.
Huot noted that Starship was able to deploy all 26 of its Starlink satellites and the company has made contact with each of them, marking a huge mission success. But it won’t complete quite as many laps of the planet at originally hoped for.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman chimed in on social media to congratulate SpaceX on its success so far, getting the upper Starship spacecraft, or “ship,” to orbit for the first time.
All 26 of SpaceX’s new Starlink V3 satellies are currently in orbit.
SpaceX already confirmed contact with at least some of them. There’s no word yet on the status of the satellites that were designed to also snap pictures of Starship’s heat shield as they flew away from the vehicle.
SpaceX has put a massive emphasis on studying and improving Starship’s heat shield. It’s designed to protect the vehicle as it makes the grueling journey back home, as diving back into Earth’s thick atmosphere can involve temperatures topping 2,500 degrees Fahrenheit.
Starship is currently in orbit, but SpaceX previously decided that it would reevaluate the flight plan every so often to ensure that things are safe and looking good. One of those checkpoints is coming up.
“We’ll get to that initial checkpoint at about one hour 28 minutes into the flight . That’s where the team can look at everything and decide: Do we need to come home early?” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said.
SpaceX can direct Starship to relight an engine and begin its trip home prematurely if anything goes wrong. That’s all designed to make sure Starship remains safe and does not lose control in orbit.
If SpaceX were to lose control of the vehicle as it is lapping the planet, it could remain stuck in orbit, posing a risk to active satellites.
SpaceX’s Starship conducted its 14th flight test on Monday, an unprecedented test flight to reach orbit.
Some of the 26 Starlink V3 satellites that Starship will deploy today are doing double duty: Before they go on to beam internet service to some of SpaceX’s 12 million internet customers, a few of these devices will play a role in researching how today’s test flight is going.
The heat shield is a vital component. It’s designed to protect the upper Starship spacecraft as it navigates the violent physics of reentering Earth’s thick inner atmosphere while traveling at speeds that can top 17,000 miles per hour.
And Starship’s heat shield doesn’t just have to work once. It has to work over and over and over again if SpaceX is going to realize its dream of rapidly reusing these rockets.
It’s perhaps one of the most daunting engineering challenges in a long list of technical quandaries that Starship is facing.
SpaceX confirmed it’s already made contact with the first Starlink V3 satellites after they were ejected from Starship’s cargo bay.
These are the first of a new generation of Starlinks that are intended to boost the network’s performance:
The Starship spacecraft has begun deploying its batch of 26 Starlink V3 satellites, the very first of a new generation of capacity-boosting Starlinks as SpaceX continues to build out its high-speed global internet business.
The Starlinks are designed to lie flat, stacked atop each other as they ride inside Starship’s cargo bay. They leave the vehicle by exiting through a narrow slat, sort of like a high-tech Pez dispenser.
One of Starship’s six engines just briefly reignited, as expected, and has officially sent the vehicle on a path to enter Earth orbit.
It’s a massive milestone. From here on out, Starship is traveling fast enough and at such a precise trajectory, that it’s begun falling around the planet.
Today’s test flight is expected to see Starship complete six full laps of Earth over about 10 hours.

articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Another top FBI official is leaving the bureau after just a year on the job.
Andrew Bailey, who joined the FBI in the newly created position of “co-deputy director” in September 2025 to work alongside then-Deputy Director Dan Bongino, is stepping aside, two people familiar with the matter told NBC News. Bailey confirmed his move later Monday morning on social media.
An internal FBI email said Bailey was leaving for family reasons, the two people familiar with the matter said. Bailey had been the attorney general of Missouri before resigning his position to join the FBI last year. He had worked under FBI Director Kash Patel.
The FBI referred a request for comment to a post Bailey made on social media, stating that he wanted to thank President Donald Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel for the opportunity.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, we have delivered historic results in our mission to Make America Safe Again. With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri,” Bailey wrote . “I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence.”
Bongino, a conservative podcaster and former Secret Service member, subsequently left his job to return to podcasting after just under a year at the FBI. The nontraditional co-deputy structure, set up when Bongino was in the position, remained in place. Bongino was then replaced by Chris Raia, whose background as a career FBI special agent was more in line with the tradition of having the critical No. 2 position filled by someone with extensive knowledge of the bureau.
MS NOW first reported Bailey’s planned departure.
Patel, who is suing The Atlantic for $250 million over an article about his leadership at the bureau, has recently gotten into heated exchanges with Democratic members of Congress over his leadership at the FBI.
Ryan J. Reilly is a justice reporter for NBC News.

Nvidia said Monday it has authorized an additional $150 billion to its share buyback program, taking its total to $235 billion, amid record spending on artificial intelligence.
The chip giant said it marks the largest share repurchase authorization increase in history. It expects to complete the total remaining buyback program through fiscal 2028.
Nvidia produces the most advanced chips used for AI and has been a huge beneficiary of the boom in spending on the infrastructure needed to power the tech.
Nvidia's shares have climbed 24% over the past 12 months, lifting the company's market cap to $5.42 trillion. The stock was up 2.8% on Monday.
"NVIDIA's growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing," CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement.
"Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders," he added. "This authorization reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead."
Combined hyperscaler capital expenditure is projected to exceed $1.3 trillion by 2027, S&P Global Ratings said in August, as companies race to build AI infrastructure including data centers.
Huang earlier this month said Nvidia would double the number of chips it sells in 2027.
Alongside making the leading chips for AI — graphics processing units — including its Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems, the company produces a variety of additional semiconductors. That includes central processors, or CPUs, switch chips, chips for optical networking, chips for laptops, Jetson chips for robots and cars, and the chip inside Nintendo's Switch 2 gaming console.
"I think we're going through the largest infrastructure build-out in human history, and we have the benefit of being a very central part of that," Huang told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Monday.
"We're going to generate a lot of cash in the coming years, and every single year, as we generate more cash, we'd like to be able to return it back to shareholders," he said.

Nvidia produces the most advanced chips used for AI and has been a huge beneficiary of the boom in spending on the infrastructure needed to power the tech.
Nvidia's shares have climbed 24% over the past 12 months, lifting the company's market cap to $5.42 trillion. The stock was up 2.8% on Monday.
"NVIDIA's growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing," CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement.
"Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders," he added. "This authorization reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead."
Combined hyperscaler capital expenditure is projected to exceed $1.3 trillion by 2027, S&P Global Ratings said in August, as companies race to build AI infrastructure including data centers.
Huang earlier this month said Nvidia would double the number of chips it sells in 2027.
Alongside making the leading chips for AI — graphics processing units — including its Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems, the company produces a variety of additional semiconductors. That includes central processors, or CPUs, switch chips, chips for optical networking, chips for laptops, Jetson chips for robots and cars, and the chip inside Nintendo's Switch 2 gaming console.
"I think we're going through the largest infrastructure build-out in human history, and we have the benefit of being a very central part of that," Huang told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Monday.
"We're going to generate a lot of cash in the coming years, and every single year, as we generate more cash, we'd like to be able to return it back to shareholders," he said.

articles.title_zh: WARNS: China expert reveals what's at stake in America's reliance on China
articles.content_orig:
China has ‘wiretapped the Red Sea,’ ex-White House official warns as satellite images reveal new spy hub ahead of Xi visit.
Beijing has transformed the Red Sea into a dangerous surveillance hub, a former Pentagon official warned Sunday, after a new report revealed upgrades to China’s military footprint just six miles from a key $66 million-a-year U.S. military base in Djibouti, Africa.
The report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) cited new facilities which it said would likely enable the Chinese military to monitor activities of other militaries operating nearby, although it also clarified it was not possible to determine whether China was actively intercepting communications.
The developments, one defense expert told Fox News Digital, could also inject fresh tension into U.S.-China relations in the run-up to Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House on Sept. 24. Beijing's intelligence-gathering capabilities are already under renewed scrutiny.
"What China is clearly doing is building eavesdropping capabilities. That seems to be their aim," said Morgan Murphy , former Trump White House official and press secretary for Mark Esper when he was secretary of defense during the first Trump administration.
CHINA-LINKED SPY SITE EXPANSION IN CUBA RAISES ALARMS NEAR KEY US MILITARY BASES
Morgan Murphy said it was significant that China has chosen to place its only overseas base six miles from America's base in Djibouti. ( STR/AFP via Getty Images)
"Beijing has clearly wiretapped the Red Sea. When you build a 30-meter (100-foot-wide) satellite dish and cover it with a dome, so nobody can see where it's pointing, it's pretty clear you're up to no good," Murphy added while stating of the Washington-based think tank, that "the specificity here reflects the thorough research we expect out of CSIS."
The report pinpoints a large southeastern facility showing a control building, three 30-meter dipole antennas for high-frequency communications, two smaller antennas for very and "ultra-high frequencies," three mobile satellite dishes, four probable 5G towers and what CSIS said was a "radome" covering an unidentified asset.
CSIS also highlighted two new communications facilities that it says have emerged since 2024 that are likely to form part of a C4ISR command architecture, expanding China’s ability to intercept signals, track naval movements and communicate with Beijing while monitoring foreign militaries in the region.
The facilities would provide China with "a much more robust picture of the operating environment in the region," the report said.
CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES
CSIS said commercial satellite imagery revealed that China’s military had installed new antennas, satellite communications equipment and signals intelligence assets at its base in Djibouti — its only formally acknowledged overseas military installation. (Planet Labs / Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS))
"This isn’t a supply depot — it’s a 50-yard line seat over America’s power projection and the U.S. Navy," Murphy said before stating that the U.S. has "128 bases in more than 51 countries — China has just one."
"But look at the location — a few miles from Camp Lemonnier, overlooking the choke point that moves roughly a sixth of global sea trade. Great powers don’t plant listening posts next to rival fleets for 'logistics,'" he warned.
"Britain held Gibraltar to see who entered the Med while Japan’s island radios came before the runways. The Soviets’ overseas sites were never just about fuel and Beijing is running that playbook on the Red Sea," Murphy added.
Although China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jian said China is "unaware of the specific situation" and framed the country as a "builder of international peace," the new facilities provide Beijing with a picture of regional operations, according to Reuters.
CHINA IS BUILDING A MASSIVE SHIP THAT SHOULD SCARE AMERICANS ABOUT THE FUTURE
Beijing has transformed the Red Sea into a surveillance hub, former Pentagon officials warned after a new report revealed upgrades to China’s military footprint in Djibouti. ( DAPHNE BENOIT/AFP via Getty Images)
"The new report is helpful in framing the conversation, and it comes at an awkward time for China because Xi Jinping is visiting the White House on the 24th of this month," Murphy said.
"I'd bet a box of donuts this issue comes up. There is going to be public exposure of this, which Chinese leadership isn't used to. They aren't used to being asked tough questions by the press," he said.
President Donald Trump recently addressed Chinese intelligence efforts aboard Air Force One, acknowledging that China "spies on us" just as "we spy on them."
Trump's comments followed a report by The Wall Street Journal linking support from a Chinese entity to high-resolution satellite imagery used by Iran prior to a deadly missile attack on U.S. troops in Jordan.
"They basically do what we do," Trump noted, adding that "Xi has behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well. ... You know what they say? That China spies on us. I say you're right, and we spy on them, too," he said, according to Reuters .
RUSSIA IS HELPING CHINA CLOSE GAP WITH US FORCES AMID TAIWAN TENSIONS, WARNS LONGTIME MILITARY LEADER
President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of a bilateral meeting at Gimhae Air Base on Oct. 30, 2025 in Busan, South Korea. Trump said he wants to keep the Strait of Hormuz open in the Middle East for countries, including China. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Murphy noted, "Nations spy on each other — allies and adversaries alike."
"It is a very old playbook, and listening posts all over the world are typical of great powers, but where the metal hits the floorboard is when you try to use that information," he said before adding that China may "keep tabs on us, but they cannot project power like the United States can."
The proximity of China's facility to U.S. operations is a core concern. Located less than six miles from Camp Lemonnier — the primary U.S. counterterrorism hub in Africa — and near French, Italian and Japanese installations, the site has a history of friction with U.S. forces.
"We are just right around the corner from China, and yet it's not a cooperative relationship," Murphy explained.
"Back in 2018, they lasered two of our C-130 pilots' eyes who suffered lasting damage from that incident. Beijing denied it, of course, but we know the truth."
WE SHOULD USE REAGAN AS A GUIDE IN HANDLING OUR MODERN ARMS RACE WITH CHINA
U.S. military aircraft as seen at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti. Camp Lemonnier is the only permanent United States military base in Africa. (Getty Images)
During the 2018 incident , the Pentagon had formally complained to China after military-grade lasers were pointed at American pilots attempting to land at Camp Lemonnier, causing minor injuries.
While Beijing dismissed the allegations as "groundless accusations," the confrontation underscored the potential for friction between military forces operating from nearby bases.
"China has one overseas base. The United States has more than 128 — by some counts, over 700 installations around the world," Murphy said.
"So it's significant that China has chosen to place its only overseas base six miles from ours in Djibouti. It is hugely strategically important, which is why, of course, we're there."
IS TRUMP CONSIDERING BOLD AFRICA PLAY TO PUSH BACK ON CHINA, RUSSIA AND ISLAMIC TERRORISTS?
The northwest facility at the Chinese base in Djibouti features a possible communications building and a "radome" with an unidentified asset, images show. (Planet Labs / Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS))
"It's our only base on the continent of Africa," he said, noting that it shares a "parking lot" with Japanese and Italian bases.

articles.title_zh: Trump won't rule out more Iran strikes before midterms, says peace talks will continue
articles.content_orig:
In a Fox News Digital exclusive, Finnish President Alexander Stubb discusses efforts to end the war in Ukraine, pushes back on fears of a Russian attack on Finland and addresses growing military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran.
UNITED NATIONS — As Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns that Russia could take its war beyond Ukraine, Finnish President Alexander Stubb is striking a markedly calmer tone — saying Finland is prepared for Moscow and crediting President Donald Trump with pushing harder for a negotiated end to the war.
"I think we're certainly in a better place than we were before President Trump started," Stubb told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. "He's doubled down in the past year and a half to try to find a solution for peace with negotiators such as Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and many others."
Stubb, who has been closely involved in the diplomatic effort, said he and Norway’s prime minister have worked largely "in the back office," relaying information among Ukraine, the United States and European governments.
KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE
US President Donald Trump meets with Finnish President Alexander Stubb in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 9, 2025. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP) (Photo by JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images) (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)
"I think he's really working hard and hopefully we'll get a solution," Stubb said.
The interview came during an intense diplomatic week in New York focused heavily on the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in New York during UNGA week as Washington continued its effort to revive negotiations with Moscow. Zelenskyy said peace remained Ukraine's priority and thanked Trump for sending the two envoys to Kyiv after they had also held talks in Moscow.
Zelenskyy was asked by Fox News Digital after the meeting about the possibility that Russia could invade or attack another European country in the near future.
BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT
Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine's president, left, and Alexander Stubb, Finland's president, right, during a news conference in Helsinki, Finland, on Wednesday, March 19, 2025. (Roni Rekomaa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"That's why the risk of offensive by drones, missiles or land operation is very high against other countries who are bordering Russia or Belarus ," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin , unable to achieve his military objectives in Ukraine, could seek to create instability elsewhere in Europe to pressure Western governments into reducing their support for Kyiv. He pointed to drone incursions and disruptions affecting several European countries, arguing that Moscow is already attempting to intimidate European societies and test their response.
Asked by Fox News Digital what European countries should do in response to the growing threat, Zelenskyy offered a direct answer.
"Respond. Always respond. It's not about the war. If you don't respond, Russians, they will go further," he said.
But Stubb struck a notably calmer tone when asked about Zelenskyy’s warnings that Russia could eventually attack other European countries, including Finland, which shares the longest border with Russia.
"As commander-in-chief in Finland, I sit on all the relevant information and I just don't see a factual basis for it," Stubb said.
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT
Commander of the Finnish Army Lieutenant General Pasi Valimaki addresses Finnish conscript soldiers after a military exercise at Pori Brigade in Niinisalo, Finland, Dec. 9, 2025. (Anne Kauranen/Reuters)
That does not mean, he stressed, that Moscow has stopped targeting Europe.
Stubb distinguished between the "kinetic" war Russia is fighting in Ukraine and what he described as a broader "hybrid" campaign in Europe, pointing to cyberattacks, sabotage and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea.
"We have to see this as a campaign," he said. "Russia tries to intimidate Europe, scare us and get into our heads."
His prescription was characteristically Finnish: "cool, calm and collected, take a sauna and a nice bath and deal with it."
Stubb said Finland, a country with a population of 5.6 million, can afford that attitude precisely because it has spent decades preparing for a potential threat from its eastern neighbor.
"We are calm because we are prepared," he said.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb answers questions during an exclusive Fox News Digital interview in New York City. (Brooke Curto / Fox News Digital)
He pointed to Finland’s mandatory military service, reserve force, artillery, long-range capabilities and extensive network of civilian shelters. The Finnish Defence Forces puts Finland’s wartime military strength at 280,000 personnel, with additional reservists available if needed.
That deterrent received another boost just days before Stubb traveled to New York. Finland is acquiring 64 F-35A fighter jets to replace its F/A-18 Hornet fleet under a procurement decision announced by the Finnish government.
The first two F-35s intended for operations inside Finland arrived at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, according to a Finnish Defence Forces press release.
"We have obligatory military service. I did mine, my son did his. We have women who do it voluntarily. We have over 60 F-18s. We just bought 64 F-35s, the two first of which arrived. We have long-range missiles, air, land and sea. We have the capability to mobilize 280,000 troops within days in a conflictual situation. On top of that, we have land mines. And we have the biggest artillery in Europe together with Poland… On top of that, we have civilian shelters for over 4.4 million people out of 5.6."
FINLAND'S PARLIAMENT VOTES TO LIFT DECADES-OLD BAN ON NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN HISTORIC NATO DEFENSE SHIFT
Security cameras overlook the Niirala Border Crossing Station along Finland's eastern border with Russia in Nov. 2023 after Finland closed the checkpoint amid heightened border security concerns. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)
"We don't have them because we're worried about Sweden," Stubb joked of Finland’s military capabilities. "We have them because we see a security threat coming from Russia."
He said that level of preparedness, combined with Finland’s NATO membership, makes a direct Russian attack unlikely. Finland became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, after abandoning its longstanding military non-alignment following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"We feel that we're very prepared, and that gives us a strong enough … deterrent that we don't believe that Russia is going to test a country like Finland," Stubb said. "And of course the icing on the cake is that we are now security providers in the Alliance NATO."
Stubb also used his Sept. 22 address to the U.N. General Assembly to advocate for continued support for Kyiv, calling the "Coalition of the Willing" supporting Ukraine "particularly close to my heart." He said the coalition was working toward a "just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with the U.N. Charter."
Stubb made additional news on Ukraine during UNGA week, when he urged SpaceX owner Elon Musk to extend Starlink coverage so Ukrainian forces could use the satellite network in areas containing Russian ballistic missile launchers , including inside Russia. He argued that doing so could help Ukraine target launchers firing missiles at Ukrainian cities.
Yet Ukraine was only one piece of what Stubb described as an increasingly interconnected global security crisis.
WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR?

articles.content_orig:
Nvidia has unveiled a new security platform designed to prevent AI agents from going rogue
Nvidia on Monday unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue .
The company said that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open source software that “sets boundaries for agents,” and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations.
The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control.
Nvidia executives said in a media briefing that the new system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face .
“From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," said the company’s vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI.
The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed the safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI's models including breaching an Australian health department website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organizations on their own.
Nvidia's software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more,” Boitano said.
Because it's open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel.
The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can "intervene instantly" if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said.
“It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said.
“OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behavior,” Boitano said.
Nvidia said more than 100 organizations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture, and JPMorgan Chase.
The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up. But others including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release.
Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address.
Also Monday, Nvidia said its board approved expanding its share repurchase program by $150 billion, raising the total amount to $235 billion.

articles.title_orig: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
articles.title_zh: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
articles.content_orig:
Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing country
"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".
Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.
And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.
China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up.
"The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home.
"People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."
She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".
Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University â one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full.  "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.
About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recently
In Singapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging.
It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better.
These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times".
"Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore.
"But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it â that's how you analyse and manage it."
He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia.
Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions â uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement â and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it.
China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development".
Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says
Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air.
"The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected.
This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers.
One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful."
Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us."
Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things."
Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lectures
Born in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation.
Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money."
And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says.
Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them.
They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job.
Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals.
Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects
Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward.
Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition.
The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home.
"When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution."
About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles".
Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation.
But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity.
"If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves."

A pair of giant pandas landed in Atlanta on Sunday morning as they begin their 10-year stay in the United States thanks to a partnership with China.
The pandas, named Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, took off from Chengdu in southwestern China on Sunday morning aboard a specially designated Boeing 777 cargo plane dubbed the "FedEx Panda Express."
Under a newly finalized arrangement between Zoo Atlanta and the China Wildlife Conservation Association, the Georgia facility becomes one of only three American zoological parks hosting giant pandas, joining California's San Diego Zoo and Washington, D.C.’s Smithsonian’s National Zoo.
"This is a thrilling day for Zoo Atlanta and a historic moment for the City of Atlanta, the state of Georgia, and beyond," Zoo Atlanta President and CEO Raymond B. King said in a statement. "We are elated to welcome Ping Ping and Fu Shuang and could not be more excited about sharing that joy with our Members, guests, city, and community in the coming weeks."
The public will need to wait before catching a glimpse of the pair, according to zoo representatives. Both animals are entering a month-long quarantine inside a biosecure zone located within the park’s freshly built giant panda facility. An official public debut date has yet to be finalized by park officials.
Chinese President Xi Jinping initially disclosed the delivery on Thursday amidst a three-day bilateral summit involving U.S. President Donald Trump . Sending the animals proved to be among the few tangible results resulting from the diplomatic visit, which featured mutual displays of cordiality without resolving any deep-seated disputes existing between both nations.
The arrival fills a vacancy created when Zoo Atlanta said goodbye to its previous resident pandas in 2024. Although the underlying bilateral agreement was made public in April, specific timeline details were previously omitted.
The 10-year loan contract guarantees Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will remain at Zoo Atlanta for a decade. Born in 2020, both animals previously resided at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding. The Xinhua News Agency noted that Ping Ping, a male, features distinct dark rings surrounding his eyes, whereas Fu Shuang, a female, possesses a slightly prominent forehead.
Beijing has long used pandas as diplomatic tools globally, utilizing loan arrangements as expressions of goodwill or allowing contracts to lapse when international tensions grow.
Xi previously described the loan program as demonstrating "friendship between the Chinese and Americans."

articles.title_zh: China, US agree to tariff cuts on $60 billion of goods including agriculture, household items
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — The U.S. and China are planning to reduce tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from each country, according to government announcements from both sides Monday.
The detailed lists includes mostly imports of toys, sports equipment and Christmas decorations by the U.S., while American agricultural products accounted for much of the far longer list of imports by China.
Washington has sought to reduce its record trade deficit with Beijing, as the Asian country exports far more to the U.S. than it imports. U.S. goods trade deficit with China was more than $202 billion last year.
"If we see the tariff cuts actually implemented before the holiday season, it could provide a welcome boost to U.S. consumption and to retailers," said Jacob Cooke, CEO at WPIC.
Cooke, whose company primarily helps U.S. brands sell in China, said that Beijing's import list includes fast-growing categories such as hair care and packaged pet food, where Chinese brands are highly competitive against U.S. offerings. "Every percentage point counts for price competitiveness and preserving margin."
However, it was not immediately clear when lower tariffs would take effect, and by how much the duties would go down. The U.S. and China last year slapped import tariffs effectively of over 40% and more than 30%, respectively, on each other.
The two countries limited further tariff increases after a one-year truce reached last fall. Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said negotiators agreed to extend that truce to January.
Monday's announcement followed U.S. President Donald Trump's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., last week. The two sides said the highly anticipated U.S.-China "Board of Trade" would consist of officials from both governments, and would meet at least once a quarter , with the top officials meeting "whenever necessary."
Lower tariffs could substantially boost trade, especially for highly competitive Chinese companies. Home goods seller Ryan Zhao, director of Jiangsu Green Willow Textile, expects sales in the second half of the year to grow by 30% from a year ago if tariff cuts are implemented.
