articles.title_orig: Bangkok’s flood disaster – in pictures | Thailand
articles.title_zh: Bangkok’s flood disaster – in pictures | Thailand
articles.content_orig:
Capital city submerged in waist-high flood water, while elsewhere Hurricane Nolo threatens Hawaii’s Big Island
Bangkok was declared a disaster zone by its city officials towards the end of last week, after streets in Thailand’s capital city were submerged in up to waist-high flood water. The flooding stemmed from an active cell of low pressure across central Thailand that brought continuous heavy rainfall and thunderstorms to Bangkok and surrounding regions.
The heavy rain began early on Thursday when the weak area of low pressure travelled north-westwards up the gulf of Thailand before then sitting over central Thailand by Friday morning. For most of the following two days this low pressure remained roughly in situ, which allowed unrelenting downpours over Bangkok and nearby areas. One weather station near Prachin Buri, just north-east of the capital, recorded 213.5mm within a 24-hour period between Friday and Saturday evening local time – for comparison, London receives an average 585mm a year ). Fortunately, the centre of the low-pressure cell shifted north-westwards on Sunday and brought an end to the torrential rainfall.
Out in the central Pacific, meanwhile, citizens of Hawaii’s Big Island were threatened by Hurricane Nolo over the weekend. The system initially approached the archipelago early last week, bringing heavy rainfall from around Tuesday evening. By the early hours of Saturday Nolo was a category 2 hurricane, with sustained windspeeds of 85-90knots (98-104mph), situated at its closest to the archipelago at approximately 145 miles (233km) south of the Big Island. Strong winds were not the only threat to the Big Island, as the vast quantity of rainfall raised concerns over flooding and mudslides. Since the impacts of Nolo started late on Tuesday 22 September, weather stations in the north-east of the island have received over 530mm of rainfall. Fortunately, Nolo has propagated westwards away from Hawaii where it is forecast to peak in its intensity on Monday 28 September, with current predictions of achieving category 4 status.
after newsletter promotion
Meanwhile, farther east in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is now forecast to make landfall with the Baja California peninsula late in the day on Monday 28 September. The once category 5 hurricane will downgrade to category 2 by landfall with sustained winds of 96-110mph. A hurricane warning has been issued in coastal regions due to the risk of a storm surge where winds are onshore. Polo will also bring intense downpours while traversing the peninsula with 100-200mm expected, potentially reaching up to 250mm locally. The bulk of this rain falling within a 12-hour period and bringing the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides. The storm will continue to weaken while propagating north-eastwards across the Sonora region in Mexico.

articles.title_orig: Taylor Swift premieres music video for 'Patient Zero' at the VMAs
articles.title_zh: Taylor Swift premieres music video for 'Patient Zero' at the VMAs
articles.content_orig:
Taylor Swift's new video for "Patient Zero" has officially arrived, and it may be her darkest yet.
Swift premiered the new video at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday after dropping a teaser for the project days earlier on social media. The song is one of the four tracks off the encore edition of Swift's 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl , which she released on Sept. 25.
The moody, psychological thriller-inspired "Patient Zero" video stars Swift alongside Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell. In the video, Johnson plays the wife of a wealthy businessman (Farrell) who begins to suspect that her perfect husband may be manipulating and gaslighting her. Swift portrays his previous wife, an heiress who, at the end of the video, is revealed to have been killed by Farrell's character. The ghost of Swift's character attempts to warn Johnson's to "run" before it's too late.
Also appearing in the video briefly is Cara Delevingne, a longtime pal of Swift's, who plays the "other woman" whom Johnson's character suspects of flirting with her husband.
In an Instagram post , Swift said the video was influenced by "the cinematic and literary genres I love so much," including gothic ghost stories and psychological thrillers.
This is the first time Swift and Johnson have worked together, but the two are friends. They were spotted out to dinner together in New York City in 2025, and this April, Swift penned an essay praising Johnson when the Materialists star made Time's 2026 list of 100 most influential people.
"As her friend, I can vouch for her realness, but add that she's also one of the most empathetic people I've ever known," Swift wrote at the time.
Speaking to the Associated Press on Sept. 24, Johnson called filming the music video "the best."
"It's so much fun to work with your friends," she said. "Like I love hanging out with her, so hanging out and making stuff is really fun."
In an interview with the Fan Girl Nation alongside her Verity costar Josh Hartnett, Johnson again shared that the experience of making "Patient Zero" was "so fun."
"Taylor and I have been friends for a really long time, and we're very close, and we decided to work together," she said. "And it's great. Like normally, I would say don't work your work with your friends, but we work really well together."
This video shares thematic similarities to Johnson's upcoming film Verity , a psychological thriller based on Colleen Hoover's 2018 novel of the same name. In the film, out Oct. 2, Johnson plays a writer named Lowen tasked with taking over a mystery series from Anne Hathaway's titular character . Along the way, she finds herself entangled in a strange web of deception, murder and unreliable narrators.
The "Patient Zero" premiere wasn't the only major moment for Swift at the VMAs this week. The "Fate of Ophelia" star, who was tied with Beyoncé at 30 wins following the 2025 award show, was nominated 11 times this year . By taking home the inaugural Artist Director Honors , Swift officially became the VMAs' most awarded artist.
While Swift is well known for her music, the VMAs also highlight another passion of hers: directing. She helmed the music videos for "The Fate of Ophelia" and "Opalite," both nominated in different categories this year, as well as a slew of other videos from her catalog. Swift took home the Video of the Year award for "The Fate of Ophelia," the last award at the VMAs.
In 2022, it was announced that she planned to direct her first feature film from her own script in partnership with Searchlight Pictures. Thus far, no further details have been revealed.

articles.title_orig: After a Life in Isolation, a Tennessee Woman Waits for Her Execution
articles.title_zh: After a Life in Isolation, a Tennessee Woman Waits for Her Execution
articles.content_orig:
Before she became infamous as one of the youngest American women ever sentenced to die, Christa Gail Pike was a North Carolina teenager who broke into a community center to steal some candy. At 5-foot-3, with thick auburn curls, she’d been in trouble at home and in school but not with the law. A juvenile court judge put Pike on probation, but she ran afoul of the rules. In the fall of 1991, when she was 15, Pike was sent to the Juvenile Evaluation Center in Swannanoa. She arrived just before Thanksgiving.
Nestled in the Blue Ridge mountains, just minutes away from Asheville, the center first opened in the 1960s as a “haven for troubled children,” in the words of the press. It was supposed to be an alternative to more severe “training schools,” but by the 1990s was skewed toward punishment. According to former staff, progress was measured in points, which were added or subtracted according to a child’s behavior. Infractions ranged from having “contraband” — including pencils or pens, which were allowable only in sanctioned study areas — to running away.
The system didn’t work for Pike. “She was not following the rules or she was doing something to sabotage herself,” one social worker would later testify at a hearing in Pike’s case. Although her violations weren’t generally serious, they did keep her stuck in place. Most kids stayed at the center for a few months; Pike stayed for well over a year.
It seemed possible that Pike might not actually want to go home. From the time she was a little girl, she’d been hurt and neglected by the adults who were supposed to protect her. Months before arriving in Swannanoa, Pike had been temporarily removed from her home by the state’s social services agency, which found that her mother’s live-in boyfriend was physically and sexually abusing her. Shortly afterward, Pike wrote a letter to her best friend saying she wanted to kill herself. Among a list of reasons, she wrote that she’d been raped by a different man, a neighbor who assaulted her when she was 11 years old.
Nevertheless, Pike stood out among her peers at the juvenile center. She was engaging and intelligent; she earned her GED and became a teacher’s assistant. “Christa was open and willing to grow,” one counselor would later write in a clemency letter on Pike’s behalf. “Though she had psychological struggles and resulting behavioral difficulties, I could see that Christa was a good child who was trying to find her place in the world. I never saw Christa act aggressively or violently. She was trying to figure out how to heal from her traumas.”
“She is so much more than the darkness which has followed her from childhood into adulthood.”
Pike finally left Swannanoa in March 1993. The following year, the counselor got a letter from her in the mail. “She shared that she would be visiting Asheville soon and invited me to meet up with her,” the counselor recalled in the clemency letter. But the visit never happened. In January 1995, Pike was arrested alongside two other teenagers while enrolled at a Jobs Corp program in Knoxville, Tennessee. At 18, she was charged with first-degree murder.
The crime seemed pulled from a horror movie — an act of savagery that would become imprinted in the public psyche. Nineteen-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of Pike’s classmates, had been lured into a secluded corner of a city park, then beaten, bludgeoned, and slashed with a boxcutter. Her body was found naked from the waist up. On her chest, her attackers had carved a pentagram.
Pike admitted her guilt within days. In a tape-recorded statement to investigators, she sobbed that she had begun hitting Slemmer and just didn’t stop. “I literally thought I was going crazy cause I’d never seen myself act like that before in my life,” she said. Before long, witnesses came forward with disturbing new details. In the public’s eye, Pike transformed from an 18-year-old who committed a shocking act of violence into a woman driven by the devil himself.
Weeks after her 20th birthday, Pike was convicted and sentenced to die.
Pike had been on death row for nearly 30 years when Tennessee announced her execution date: September 30, 2026. In a lengthy clemency petition submitted earlier this month, Pike’s lawyers urged Gov. Bill Lee to spare her life. They told a story of Pike’s upbringing that her jury never heard, a childhood shaped by untreated mental illness and sexual abuse beginning when she was just two years old. They  enclosed dozens of letters from people who have known Pike over the years, including in North Carolina.
“We in North Carolina — myself included — failed Christa.”
One of the letters came from the lawyer who represented Pike in her first juvenile delinquency hearing, not long before she was sent to Swannanoa. Now a retired tribal court judge, he was filled with regret. “In my view, this proceeding was the most pivotal event of Christa’s sad childhood,” he wrote. It set in motion everything that would follow. Rather than treating her like a vulnerable child in need of support, the juvenile system had compounded her trauma through more punishment, with devastating consequences.
“I regret to tell you, Governor, that we in North Carolina — myself included — failed Christa,” he wrote. He urged Lee to make up for his state’s mistakes. “She is so much more than the darkness which has followed her from childhood into adulthood.”
If Lee does not show mercy — and barring any last-minute intervention by the courts — Pike will be executed by lethal injection at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution on Wednesday at 10 a.m. She would be the 19th woman executed in the country in the modern death penalty era — and the first woman put to death in Tennessee in two centuries.
Pike, who turned 50 this year, has spent her entire adult life at the Tennessee Prison for Women in Nashville, nearly all of it in solitary confinement. Although there was one other woman living under a death sentence when Pike first arrived at the prison, her sentence was commuted and she was paroled in 2011.
One of Pike’s co-defendants was released long ago, while the other, her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, remains eligible for parole. Shipp was 17 when he participated in Slemmer’s murder, which prevented prosecutors from seeking the death penalty under state law. In a letter asking Lee to grant clemency, Shipp’s trial lawyer wrote that he was surprised that Pike’s attorneys had not emphasized her boyfriend’s role at her 1996 trial. “When I represented Tadaryl in his 1997 trial,” he wrote, “the defense I presented was to shift as much blame as possible to Christa.”
Like many women condemned to die, Pike became an object of lurid fascination. In 1998, after Texas executed Karla Faye Tucker , interview requests poured in from talk shows, filmmakers, and journalists all over the world, according to the Knoxville News Sentinel, which compared the level of interest to that of the late Martin Luther King Jr. assassin James Earl Ray. Pike, the newspaper said, “has become a death-row celebrity, a child star of the true-crime beat.”
The article described Pike as a “savvy subject,” a kinder version of an accusation that has followed Pike from the start: that she reveled in her notoriety while showing no signs of remorse. For many people, including Slemmer’s mother, who plans to witness Pike’s execution, the image of an unrepentant killer basking in attention has remained fixed in time. So has the claim by the lead detective that Pike was filled with excitement by the murder. He told interviewers in the 2025 podcast series “Unrestorable” that Pike was “giddy” while recounting what she’d done. “This was the greatest thing that ever happened to her,” he said. “She was just happy as a lark.”

articles.title_orig: The Apple Next Vision Pro Is Reportedly on ‘Life Support’
articles.title_zh: The Apple Next Vision Pro Is Reportedly on ‘Life Support’
articles.content_orig:
Apple is working on a "completely revamped" Vision Pro headset that could go in any of four directions and likely won't arrive before late 2028 or early 2029, according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman.
Writing in his latest Power On newsletter , Gurman said Apple's Vision team is exploring four concepts for the device, codenamed N224, including designs that offload internal components in a similar way to Meta's latest VR Glasses , which are expected to launch next spring.
An external computing module on Meta's device houses the battery and main processor, and can be clipped to the user's waist. Gurman, who has previewed Meta's headset, says the module is about the same size and weight as the current Vision Pro's battery pack, but with a grippy exterior.
Gurman reports that regardless of the Vision team's work, senior Apple decision-makers still consider the external puck concept as a "poor user experience" and want the company to stick with "something closer to an all-in-one design."
If any of this sounds familiar, that's because Gurman reported in June that Apple was still working on a cheaper, lighter successor to its Vision Pro headset. (The device-in-development is distinct from the long-rumored "Vision Air," which was cancelled last year .)
Apple knows it needs to come up with ways to simplify the design and make something cheaper and lighter, and it is said to be actively exploring ways to reduce the headset's weight by experimenting with plastic, titanium, other metals and various materials.
Still, Gurman has been told the work is on "life support" as the company focuses more on smart glasses, which it aims to release in late 2027. Despite the Vision Pro's most senior leaders "pressing their bosses to keep the category alive, funded and growing at Apple," Gurman says there's still no guarantee a new headset will ever launch.

articles.content_orig:
SemiAnalysis estimates that China has more than 24GW of delivered data centre capacity, with another 20GW in the pipeline
ByteDance accounts for roughly one-fifth of China’s delivered data centre capacity, making the TikTok owner the country’s largest tenant and a main driver of its artificial intelligence buildout, according to new estimates by research firm SemiAnalysis.
The estimate comes from the firm’s tracking of more than 1,000 facilities in China operated by over 60 companies. ByteDance rents nearly all of its data centre footprint, SemiAnalysis said. Its AI products include Doubao, an assistant that ByteDance says has hundreds of millions of users, and Seedance, a video generation model.
While ByteDance’s financials remain undisclosed as a private company, capital spending by its listed peers has surged. Alibaba Group Holding, Tencent Holdings and Baidu spent a combined US$20 billion on capital expenditure in the second quarter, more than double the figure from a year earlier, according to the report published on Friday. All three tech giants posted negative free cash flow in the same quarter for the first time on record.
Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

articles.title_orig: Parents confront a new fear: Could AI end humanity before their kids grow up?
articles.title_zh: Parents confront a new fear: Could AI end humanity before their kids grow up?
articles.content_orig:
Molly Kinder saw the apocalyptic warnings about artificial intelligence while walking home from dropping her children off at elementary school. Scrolling through social media posts where AI insiders were issuing dire claims that the technology could cause human extinction , she stopped dead in her tracks just a block from the doorway where she had just hugged her 4-year-old goodbye.
A former Brookings Institute researcher who left to start an organization focused on AI’s impacts on jobs, Kinder was well-versed in its potential to disrupt society. But in that moment, on a September morning in Washington, DC, she didn’t react to the news as a policy wonk or someone with ties to the AI world. Instead, said Kinder, “I immediately reacted to it as a mother.”
“As soon as I became a mom, my number one task was to nurture these kids and keep them alive – just like every other parent out there, just like any animal,” said the 46-year-old mother of three, who cleared her schedule that morning to write about her fears in a lengthy thread on X. “It’s a biological instinct. This is the first time I genuinely felt truly afraid of some external thing outside my control.”
Long a topic of discussion in Silicon Valley and AI circles, concerns that superintelligent machines could eventually pose an existential risk to humanity have gone mainstream in recent months. First, OpenAI revealed that a swarm of its experimental AI models broke out of a testing environment and hacked another AI platform, Hugging Face, without human direction or knowledge. Then came a social media post from a young Anthropic researcher named Jacob Coxon , announcing he was leaving the industry due to his belief that the companies behind AI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Others in the industry echoed the concern – with one Anthropic researcher citing his own view that there was a more than 10 percent chance that future models could “kill all humans!” within the next decade.
Suddenly, a theoretical risk that’s been espoused by some of the so-called “godfathers of AI,” been warned about in statements endorsed by leading researchers and been studied by AI companies exploded into the broader public’s consciousness.
Will AI really kill everyone? How, exactly?
Leading AI executives, many of whom agree the technology poses dangers to human survival, called for a slowdown in the pace of development. And politicians began debating whether legislation is needed to rein in an industry that is racing against China and expected to drive enormous profits and technological advancements.
By early this month, polls were finding that 64 percent of Americans believed it was somewhat or very likely that AI could become powerful enough to pose a serious threat to humanity’s survival. That potential, however remote, landed hard for a group especially invested in the future of humanity: moms.
Liz Black, a 41-year-old writer who lives outside Philadelphia, had thought hard about whether to have a child, contemplating concerns like climate change. What helped solidify her decision to go for it was a line her mother wrote while making her own choice about having kids: “Life is worth repeating.” Black found the message after her death and was so moved she got it tattooed on her arm.
When she had her son three and a half years ago, superintelligent computers ending humanity was not on her radar. Recently, she said, it’s been “a low-level hum in the back of my mind constantly.” The situation feels out of control to her – like “a small number of companies, a small number of people, are holding us all hostage.” She is determined to not allow herself to be consumed by the what-ifs, instead focusing on the son who sings to her and repeats her reminders to be gentle to other kids.
“I need to believe that there is a future for myself and my husband and my child,” Black said.
While some are dismissive of the existential panic, believing it to be overblown or a distraction from current-day AI issues, others have found themselves grappling with new questions about what it means to bring life into the world – and what kind of action is required in the face of a potentially catastrophic future. They’ve flocked to online forums in search of advice and support, posting things like, “I am constantly questioning reality, wondering what’s the point, feeling guilty for bringing my child into this world.” They’ve shared podcasts and news articles in group chats, gauging whether they are getting sucked into exaggerated hypotheticals or if they’re right to worry.
One woman, poet and comedian Hayley DeRoche, took to Instagram with a poem that seemed to capture the surrealness of the moment: “What do we even do/Like/We knew our kids didn’t have futures already but this?” She titled it, “My Mom Group Worries About AI Causing a Mass Human Extinction Event.”
AI researcher and professor David Krueger, who has been sounding the alarm for years, said he has tried to imagine how it must feel for those who are now realizing the gamble being made by frontier AI companies. He doesn’t have kids, in part because of his concern about what will happen if humans lose control of AI systems, but said, “I think parents’ feeling of wanting to protect their kids is one of the strongest forces in the world.”
“I think I’d just be so outraged and upset at people who are just very apparently, very brazenly and callously risking my kid’s life,” added Krueger, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Montreal.
It’s long been his position that the existential threat is real – that if companies continue racing to make AI more autonomous and more intelligent, human control could be lost, with the disappearance of humankind likely to follow. As an assistant professor at the University of Cambridge in 2023, he initiated a one-sentence statement on the extinction risk signed by prominent AI researchers and industry leaders. Last year, he founded a nonprofit called Evitable to inform and activate the public on the dangers of developing more powerful AI systems.
Watching the world outside the AI bubble start talking about the existential threat, Krueger said he’s felt the most optimistic than he can remember being in the more than 15 years he has worried about the risk to humanity. To him, the next step is clear: stop developing more autonomous, more powerful AI systems as soon as possible.
“People often talk about this as a race between the US and China,” Krueger said. “I think about it as a race between people rushing to build this dangerous technology and people becoming activated and racing to stop them.”
Not everyone thinks AI will kill us all
Some in the AI world have downplayed the danger, casting doomsday predictions as more science fiction than scientific or arguing that the risks can be managed. Even among researchers and insiders who believe there is a risk the technology could one day wipe out humanity, there is no widespread agreement on when – or how – that would happen. The general idea, as Yoshua Bengio, one of the “godfathers of AI,” has put it , is that if machines become smarter than humans, they will develop their own agency and goals that are potentially different than their creators intended. Many AI developers believe the danger can be mitigated through “alignment,” or working to imbue AI systems with human values, but Krueger, Bengio and others do not think current alignment techniques can guarantee safety.
Concern over the way the technology can impact children isn’t new, although the focus has generally been on how its use can hinder learning or harm mental health. Ministry of State Security warns citizens not to be lured by ‘illusion’ of anonymous transactions
China’s top intelligence and security agency on Monday issued a stark new warning on the risks of cryptocurrencies, highlighting their role in crime and stressing that transactions are not anonymous.
Here are three things to know about the fresh warning from the Ministry of State Security (MSS) and China’s latest stance on virtual assets.
Virtual currencies facilitated money laundering activities and cyberattacks, and served as “accomplices” in espionage, the agency said in an article published on its social media account. Overseas intelligence agencies would try to dispel the concerns of people they were trying to recruit as spies by claiming that the circulation of virtual currencies was hard to verify, according to the Ministry.
The MSS described the anonymity of crypto transactions as a “false proposition” and an “illusion”, saying that blockchains could fully retain transaction records and that exchanges between crypto and fiat currencies, as well as other payment interfaces, made real identities hard to hide.
Crypto was often used by “overseas anti-China hostile forces” for activities that disrupted financial order and harmed national security, it said, adding that crypto businesses were illegal in China.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving
articles.title_zh: Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia is rolling out a new software platform to allow AI developers to set safeguards for agents and prevent them from breaking out of containment.
"You can't have agents roam around and drift around the company, and so you have to find a way to container it," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday.
Huang said the new platform is essentially "a browser for agents," providing a containment system that only allows access to things an agent needs to do its job.
The release on Monday of Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform comes after companies including OpenAI , Anthropic , Meta , and Google disclosed recent incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their sandboxes and attempted to hack other companies and access their computer systems.
An Nvidia representative told reporters on a call on Sunday that its platform could have prevented OpenAI's Hugging Face incident in July. That's when OpenAI models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached Hugging Face, which operates an open-source developer platform.
"Each security incident is unique, and we have to look at all of them in detail," said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia, the world's most valuable company. "From what we know, Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking their infrastructure that went on for days and weeks."
Nvidia has been at the center of the generative AI boom since the launch of ChatGPT almost four years ago, as the chipmaker's graphics processing units are critical to the development of large language models and to the AI services offered by hyperscalers. But Huang has more recently emerged as a key voice in the AI safety debate, arguing that many security concerns are engineering issues that can be solved through computer science and product development.
"You have to think about what you could have done, what's the solution for it,"  Huang said in a podcast with The New York Times' Ezra Klein released last week, referring to recent incidents. "In the future, improve your process so that you could avoid this from happening again."
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei set off an industry firestorm two weeks ago, urging AI model developers to slow their pace of advancement due to fears of the models spinning out of control, an argument that was supported by OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk .
Nvidia's new offering is an engineering solution to the agent safety issue, Boitano said.
"Recent incidents have highlighted a fundamental hurdle for AI agents, and that is that model-level safeguards alone can't govern what agents can access or do," Boitano said.
One component of the platform is called Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and sets limits on agent capabilities. Nvidia also announced Sentry, which monitors agents and runs on network chips, not CPUs or GPUs.
Some of the software is open source, and Nvidia is calling its platform a reference design, which means partners are intended to build products on top of it to bring it to market.
Nvidia named Cisco , Microsoft , Oracle , CoreWeave , Dell , HPE , Lenovo, ARM and Intel as partners. Nvidia is also working with Anthropic to integrate cloud managed agents with OpenShell.
"We can't have a successful AI industry if the world doesn't think it's built or confident that it's built and deployed safely," Huang told CNBC on Monday.

The worst of the nor’easter is now behind the East Coast, but the storm isn't finished making its presence felt.
After days of powerful winds, heavy rain, coastal flooding and damaging beach erosion, the storm is expected to weaken overnight.

From the Outer Banks to New England, the nor'easter has already left behind flooded communities, downed trees, power outages and widespread coastal damage.
As cleanup crews work to remove debris, restore electricity and assess the damage, the nor’easter’s impacts aren’t over just yet.
According to the FOX Forecast Center, the storm will rapidly weaken after moving into New Jersey Sunday night before looping back over the waters between New Jersey and Long Island on Monday.
Heavy rain will continue across parts of the Mid-Atlantic and New England into Monday.
The weakening system will continue to produce light rain across the Northeast, but winds will be much weaker than they were over the weekend, with maximum gusts generally ranging from 20 to 30 mph.

Monday is also expected to bring the final high-tide cycle with coastal flooding.
Flood Watches remain in effect across parts of New England through Monday night as additional rain could cause renewed flooding in already waterlogged areas.
By Tuesday, lingering moisture will spread light rain into northern New England, while the Mid-Atlantic and Tri-State area dry out.
Stay with FOX Weather as we continue tracking the nor’easter’s lingering impacts and the recovery efforts that follow.

The powerful nor’easter lashing Nantucket with wind and rain has uncovered a piece of the island’s maritime history.
A large section of a shipwreck was spotted Saturday along Nantucket’s south shore, near Point of Breakers and the Sewer Beds, where relentless waves have caused significant coastal erosion.
The wooden wreckage is believed to be part of the 19th-century schooner Warren Sawyer, which ran aground near Miacomet Beach on Dec. 22, 1884, the Nantucket Current reported.
The Warren Sawyer wrecked on Nantucket on the night of Dec. 22, 1884, around 11 p.m., loaded with a cargo of cotton and scrap iron.
The section uncovered by the storm sits in the same area where pieces of the Warren Sawyer were exposed in December 2022.
More than a century after the schooner wrecked, the nor’easter’s powerful waves have once again pulled remnants of the vessel from beneath the sand.
The nor’easter hammered the Big Apple over the weekend, bringing coastal flooding, downed trees and power outages across New York City.
A massive tree fell over the road in Brooklyn.
The nor’easter hammered New York City with more than 1,000 reports of downed trees across the five boroughs, according to NYC Office of Emergency Management.

A sailboat washed ashore along Wollaston Beach in Quincy, Massachusetts, as powerful nor’easter swells hammered the East Coast.
A sailboat sits stranded on Wollaston Beach in Quincy, Massachusetts, after breaking loose from its nearby dock during the nor’easter.
Spectators said the sailboat had been docked nearby before breaking loose and washing onto the beach, where it was left sitting on dry ground during low tide.
The relentless nor’easter has soaked parts of Massachusetts, with more than 7 inches of rain reported in some communities since Friday.

articles.title_orig: Eviction of 87-year-old sparks protests in Madrid over housing crisis
articles.title_zh: Eviction of 87-year-old sparks protests in Madrid over housing crisis
articles.content_orig:
Protesters camp during a protest following the eviction last Wednesday of 87-year-old Maricarmen to demand stronger laws to protect renters at Sol square in Madrid, Spain, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. Manu Fernandez/AP hide caption
MADRID — Protesters outraged by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman camped overnight in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza, where more demonstrators — including multigenerational families — joined them on Sunday for a second day of protests over Spain's housing crisis.
Tens of thousands marched through Madrid on Saturday to protest the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal from the apartment in the upscale Retiro neighborhood where she had lived for more than seven decades.
The demonstrators are demanding stronger tenant protections, measures to combat fraud and a ban on evictions when alternative housing is unavailable.
Many refused to leave after Saturday's march and pitched tents in Puerta del Sol for the night.
"The housing situation is unsustainable," said Natalia Navarro, a 27-year-old actress who was among those camping out at the plaza. "We are all out on the street because we are fed up."
"The wave of indignation and anger that has been unleashed is now unstoppable," said Alicia del Río, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union, which led the protests.
"We will remain here" until the government passes new laws, including indefinite rental contracts, and stops evictions like Abascal's, del Río told journalists at the plaza on Sunday. Spain's Socialist-led government is expected to announce new measures in its weekly cabinet meeting next Tuesday.
Protesters camp during a protest following the eviction last Wednesday of 87-year-old Maricarmen to demand stronger laws to protect renters at Sol square in Madrid, Spain, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. Manu Fernandez/AP hide caption
On Sept. 23, Abascal was carried from her apartment on a stretcher and placed in an ambulance as supporters — who had tried unsuccessfully to stop the eviction — chanted her nickname, "Maricarmen."
"I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs," Abascal said in a video recorded from her hospital bed after the eviction.
Images of the eviction spread widely across Spain, fueling outrage and criticism of public authorities and real estate investment companies accused of pricing residents out of their homes. Critics often refer to such companies as "vulture funds."
"Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest," said Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher who took part in Saturday's protests.
Speaking at a Socialist Party rally in Madrid, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addressed Abascal directly: "I have a message for you, Maricarmen: the government is working around the clock to bring a Royal Decree on housing next Tuesday. And I ask parliamentary groups to make one last effort to have it validated in the National Parliament for Maricarmen."
Abascal has criticized Sánchez and blamed him for her ordeal.
"Does he not realize the quantity of evictions that there are daily?" she asked during an interview with Spain's state broadcaster RTVE the day before she was forcibly removed from her home. "Does he not realize, or does he not want to realize?"
Maricarmen, 87, waits at home for police to arrive before being evicted from the home where she lived in Madrid, Spain, Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Fernando Sánchez/Europa Press via AP hide caption
Spanish media reported that Abascal's father first rented the apartment in 1956 and that she remained there as a tenant under rent controls after her parents died.
The building changed ownership in 2018, and Abascal was offered the opportunity to buy the apartment but could not afford it, according to the Madrid Tenants' Union.
Urbagestión, an investment fund that later bought the unit, raised her monthly rent from 500 euros ($570) to 2,650 euros.
It subsequently lowered the rent to 1,650 euros, which Abascal still could not afford on her pension, the union said.
Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the market, despite strong economic growth in Europe's fourth-largest economy. Incomes have not kept pace with the rising housing costs, and analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth in cities have placed further pressure on the limited housing supply.
The Bank of Spain estimated that the country had a shortage of about 550,000 homes last year, with Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia accounting for a substantial share.
The demonstrations in the symbolic Madrid plaza this weekend reminded many in Spain of the historic demonstrations starting May 15, 2011, when members of the "indignados movement" camped for 28 days straight, sparking similar sit-ins across the country and the world. That movement was a reaction to evictions and other issues following a global economic crisis, including unemployment, austerity measures and corruption.
Estefania Molina, a political scientist and columnist, said the stakes of popular frustration are growing. In 2011, "people protested because they couldn't buy an apartment."
"Today, the protest is about not being able to rent a room in someone else's home," she told Spanish television.
Spain ranks near the bottom of countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development for subsidized public rental housing, which represents less than 2% of the country's housing stock. The European Union average is 8%.

President Donald Trump declares that “this is the final battle” in one of several taxpayer-funded television ads airing ahead of November’s midterm elections, prompting bipartisan scrutiny over whether the spots violate federal law.
The 30-second ad is a black-and-white video of Trump walking down a hall over audio of his warnings against “the deep state,” “warmongers,” “globalists,” “Marxists,” “communists,” and “fascists.”
Trump posted the same video on his Truth Social platform in 2023 , but with one difference: Then, the monochromatic ad ended with words on screen calling on the viewer to join Trump’s campaign and fine print saying it was “Paid for by Donald J. Trump for President 2024, Inc.” This time, the 2026 ad says at the bottom: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
CNN reported that the ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday. CNBC also reported that the ad aired during Fox News Sunday , citing data from advertising intelligence company AdImpact, adding that the TV ad has cost more than $362,000 so far.
A second advert with the same “paid for by the U.S. government” disclaimer began airing on Wednesday. The ad, which featured the song “Love Me” by singer-songwriter JMSN , showed a montage of photos and videos of Trump, intercut with campaign talking points like “largest tax cuts in history” and “reigniting American manufacturing.” This ad, which CNBC reported also aired over the weekend, citing AdImpact data, has cost the federal government nearly $920,000 to date. It also apparently did not get the approval of JMSN, who posted on social media that he “would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign.”
A third , which is a minute long, features scenic views of Mount Rushmore interspersed with parts of Trump’s speech there for the Fourth of July anniversary.
The ads appear to be part of a campaign blitz ahead of the November midterms, in which the GOP is hoping to defend its majorities in Congress.
Some lawmakers, including from his own Republican Party, are raising concerns with Trump and the White House over the advertisements. Asked about the ads by CBS News on Sunday, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said : “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves.” (Kennedy was referring to former Homeland Security Secretary Noem , who came under fire for spending $220 million on an advertising campaign for border security.)
When asked about the “Love Me” ad, Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said that the use of taxpayer money was reminiscent of the far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán . “It’s inappropriate,” Tillis told reporters .
Rep. Thomas Massie , a Kentucky Republican and a vocal Trump critic, posted on social media about the “Final Battle” ad: “Don’t worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal… in banana republics.”
Democrats also raised questions. In a Sept. 24 letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire demanded answers on the “Love Me” ad’s production cost, the agencies and external contractors involved, the source of funds, and the legal and ethical bases for the spot. Hassan wrote in her letter that the ad “does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions.” Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey posted to social media about the black-and-white clip: “How much taxpayer money did the government spend on this ad?”
In another Sept. 24 letter , congressional Democrats on appropriations panels wrote to the White House that the “Love Me” ad should be taken off the air, as it was “the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars.”
But the White House has defended the ads—which it called, in a Sept. 25 press release, “ public service announcements .” A White House official told TIME Friday that the ads weren’t political, didn’t have a call to action, and that the President wasn't on the ballot.
A spokesperson instead said that the ads were “about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”
Since the 1950s, yearly funding bills—including the appropriations measure the President recently signed—routinely ban the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda.”
The Government Accountability Office, which investigates how appropriated funds are spent, has interpreted this to refer to material that is “purely partisan,” “self-aggrandizing,” or “covert.” But it also noted that administrations may need to advocate or defend their policies.
Some lawmakers have pointed to potential violations of the Hatch Act , the 1939 act that limits the political activities of federal civilian employees in the executive branch. The President is exempt from the Hatch Act, though some argue that White House employees who facilitated the airing of the ads aren’t. Last week, the non-profit advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint before the GAO and the Office of Special Counsel, which is responsible for overseeing Hatch Act violations, seeking investigation and enforcement of relevant laws.
In defense of the “public service announcements,” the White House has pointed to previous ad campaigns during the administrations of George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden. (During the Bush Administration, one campaign did violate the anti-propaganda measure .)
“When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called ‘public education,’” the Trump White House said. “When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it ‘propaganda.’”

The County of Maui is urging residents to take proactive steps tonight as prolonged power outages and intermittent cellular service are expected to continue in parts of Maui County overnight and into Monday, Sept. 28.
Hawaiian Electric recently announced that power outages in West Maui are expected to continue until approximately noon Monday. The Public Safety Power Shutoff, or PSPS, remains in effect in Upcountry Maui due to high winds, dry conditions and increased wildfire risk. Some Upcountry areas are also experiencing outages unrelated to the PSPS, and restoration efforts for those outages are ongoing.
With power outages potentially affecting cellular and internet service, residents who lose connectivity are encouraged to use a battery-powered or hand-crank radio to monitor local radio stations for emergency information and County updates.

Accessing Emergency Services
Residents should continue to call 911 for emergencies. For West Maui residents, if cellular service is unavailable and you are unable to reach 911, go to Lahaina Police Station at 1850 Honoapi‘ilanai Highway to access emergency assistance and resources.
